utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone after a relatively long break. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Perhaps for the new start, we go through the routine and ask the appearances for Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Alan Tieger and Tim Resch appear on behalf of the Prosecution, assisted by case manager, Carmela Javier,

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May it please Your Honour. I appear with my learned friend Ms. Loukas, as before, and Ms. Tatjana Cmeric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then, for the record, you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, I personally am Nicholas Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, just for the record, Mr. Stewart. Before the longer break, we finished the examination-in-chief of Mr. Treanor. Is the Defence ready to cross-examine Mr. Treanor?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. May I just make two comments. First of all, my apologies, Your Honour, that we have kept the Court waiting a few minutes. We had some unexpected security problems this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The second point is this, Your Honour: I have mentioned to Mr. Harmon, who is not here personally at the moment, a point. I don't want to go into what the point is, but I have mentioned an issue which I do wish to raise at some stage in front of the Tribunal, not this morning. Mr. Harmon knows about it. I'm sure Mr. Tieger knows about it as well, actually. I simply wanted to say this: That because it does -- I have had correspondence with the Chief Prosecutor, Mrs. Del Ponte, and it's not impossible that I may make some criticism of Mrs. Del Ponte, I do wish to say that I'm not going to raise it today. If it is felt that Ms. Del Ponte wishes to be in Court when I raise this point then I invite the Prosecution to let me know. I shall assume not, in which case it's likely that I shall raise the matter at the beginning of some session during the course this week, probably when we finish with Mr. Treanor. It's not immediately urgent; on the other hand, it's something that shouldn't be left for too long. But I didn't want to be discourteous and I didn't want it to be said then that if I do make any criticism that Mrs. Del Ponte should have had the opportunity of being here. She has that opportunity. If the Prosecution would like to let me know and then if she does, then we could arrange a suitable day. Because I know she is a very busy lady.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, if you give notice well in advance and I think it belongs to the good manners in court to indicate that you might have some criticism of someone, although I can imagine that someone being criticised could not always be present in this courtroom, certainly she should have the possibility to attend. Then if there are no other issues, Mr. Usher, would you please escort Mr. Treanor into the courtroom. Yes, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. If I may have five minutes, by your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it would be five minutes, then we'd rather not have Mr. Treanor in yet, unless it's directly related to Mr. Treanor. But I don't think so. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I would like to thank you for the attention you have dedicated to this trial, Your Honours. I find it encouraging that you have dedicated a lot of attention to this trial, more, if I may say, then we see in other trials, and I hope we can reach the truth, which is the main objective of this trial. However, I do have a proposal to make to expedite proceedings in this trial. It may be a little criticism too. I believe the interpreters are not interpreting this trial sufficiently well. I do not know English myself; however, when Mr. Treanor read from a Serbian document and translated the Serbian document directly into English, then I was receiving interpretation and I realised that the meaning of the document was entirely different from what I was receiving. I assume this may also happen when proceedings are being interpreted into English. I did manage to find a reason for the interpreters going wrong on that particular document. Many of the participants in this trial speak very fast, and Mr. Treanor too was speaking fast at that time. That may have been why the interpreters got it wrong, and I think the meaning of their interpretation was entirely wrong. This provided a motive for me -- I do not mean hereby to complain about the interpreters. A recording of that trial was published in Republika Srpska through an agency that follows these trials, and what was said was that Mr. Krajisnik wanted and proposed to go to war, whereas the meaning of the original document was entirely different. It is in relation to this that I would like to see more attention devoted to the issues of interpretation in this trial. And secondly, I would like to ask the following: There is an agency here that has an exclusive right to all interpretations being made in these trials. May they please come to us and see our team so that it would be made possible for us to communicate with the public and to help to establish the truth. I believe it would be very helpful for everyone in Bosnia and Herzegovina and Republika Srpska to know these are the people who are made to answer, and this is what they're being charged with. The comments made by this agency, the name of the agency is Sense, are quite mistaken and erroneous. Another thing that I wish to raise is the following: The Registry has curtailed the funds for our defence, which makes it increasingly difficult for us to prepare our defence. They said that I was actually not in debt in relation to come credits that they spoke about. I asked to have a certificate from the Registry to certify either that I'm able to finance my own defence or, on the contrary, that the funds be raised, because there is a lot that remains to be done. The OTP sent out into the field an entire army of their investigators, and they're going to each and every one of our witnesses directly, asking them to give statements. As a result, they are under pressure because they tell each and every one of the witnesses that they themselves are under suspicion, therefore people refuse to testify in this case, and we ourselves have not sufficient funds to organise for this to go and see each and every one of the witnesses ourselves. Last but not least I personally do not believe that my defence team is prepared to cross-examine Mr. Treanor. I went it through the materials myself, through the documents. I know what the situation is because I lived in the area, after all. There is a massive amount of documents and I know what we're dealing with. I know it is in my best interest to expedite proceedings, but if we do it thoroughly, I believe things might be better understood in Bosnia and Herzegovina once this trial is completed. I believe it would be necessary to postpone the cross-examination of Mr. Treanor for at least another month. In this way, Your Honours, it will be easier for you to expedite this trial. I don't think it will truly contribute to a speed-up proceedings if we just deal with this witness quickly. As I asked at the beginning, and thank you for helping me to give my own contribution to establish the -- to establishing the truth, if I may be allowed, once the testimony of Mr. Treanor is over, to help and elucidate on a number of points. I'm sure this will only go to help you establish your verdict and reach the final truth. Thank you very much for granting me this opportunity to just address you with a couple of words. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Krajisnik. Yes, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, this is not --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It isn't the usual situation where counsel has informed the Court that he's ready to cross-examine and then his client says very directly to the Tribunal and therefore in effect to me that he's not. I should say, I don't believe any of this creates any enormous personal tensions between Mr. Krajisnik and me, but it's clearly not an entirely happy situation. Just thinking on my feet for the moment, which is also part of my job, how to reconcile the position. It wouldn't be any surprise to the Tribunal that what Mr. Krajisnik has just said reflects, of course, private discussions which have taken place. The Tribunal would be astonished if this were the first time that Mr. Krajisnik had ever expressed any such a view and had taken me totally by surprise. I don't suggest that that has happened. I don't need to go into any of those discussions, but it will be plain that they have taken place. The -- we suggest, with respect, that the appropriate way to deal with this would be as follows: That I should proceed, notwithstanding Mr. Krajisnik's remarks, that I should proceed with cross-examination of Mr. Treanor, because I'm confident that there is a considerable amount of ground that can be adequately covered, notwithstanding Mr. Krajisnik's concerns about lack of preparation. However, I do acknowledge, recognise, that -- and I say on Mr. Krajisnik's behalf that Mr. Krajisnik has done a very great deal of work on Mr. Treanor's evidence, and he's done a very great deal of detailed work, because Mr. Krajisnik is, if he wouldn't be embarrassed by my saying so, we would suggest that Mr. Krajisnik is probably far better than averagely equipped to do such work than many defendants who appear in front of this Tribunal. And he does do that work. This gives us -- there is, of course, a general point in relation to this as well, of which the Tribunal is aware. This does give us a considerable amount of extra work, about which in a sense we don't complain because most lawyers welcome having a client who takes an active interest and does provide them with active instructions. But he does produce a great deal of work, and Mr. Krajisnik writes all his material, of course, in Serbian, which means that there's only one immediate member of our team with such assistance as we can muster who is able to deal with that, so that we can then digest it. So it is an enormous burden. Getting to the point, Your Honour: We do feel that it's likely that we would get to the position some point, therefore, in the next two or three days of saying: Well, there is potentially further cross-examination of Mr. Treanor arising out of particularly work which Mr. Krajisnik has done and relating to his concerns. Now, at least with Mr. Treanor, we are in the position where he doesn't go back to Republika Srpska or he doesn't go back to another part of Bosnia and Herzegovina and has to be brought back and forwards all the time. At least Mr. Treanor from a purely practical view is, as we understand it, generally reasonably available as long as practical arrangements have been made. Therefore it seems, and it will be a matter of application at an appropriate point and judgement for the Tribunal, but looking ahead, it seems that we would get to that point at some stage where Mr. Krajisnik would clearly feel far more comfortable and with reason, Your Honour, because even over the last few days Mr. Krajisnik has done more work on the matter and we have received more detailed material from him and there are actually limits to how quickly that can be absorbed. So what I propose -- I'm not -- I should make it clear to the Tribunal, and perhaps indirectly to Mr. Krajisnik, that I'm not happy with a proposal under which I conduct part of the cross-examination, then effectively Mr. Krajisnik conducts part of the cross-examination himself. That wouldn't seem to be as a method of proceeding in this Tribunal ultimately helpful to the Tribunal, to Mr. Krajisnik, or in fact to me on behalf of Mr. Krajisnik. It would be much more satisfactory to have time so that Mr. Krajisnik then himself felt sufficiently confident that his Defence team had been briefed and instructed by him, so that they could then do -- complete the cross-examination. Your Honour, that's given where we are and given the comments that our own client has made this morning, I suggest that that is the appropriate course. I've indicated -- I know the Tribunal of course as a Tribunal always does, wants to know about timetable and scheduling and so on. The best I could indicate to the Prosecution team before Easter was that I expected to take, for practical purposes, all or most of this week with Mr. Treanor, and I was aware that if they needed -- if they brought a witness before the end of this week, that witness might be hanging around until next week before actually coming into court. Naturally, I undertook to the Prosecution in the normal way to update them continually on where I had got to, and I wouldn't be absolutely sure that we would need the whole of the week anyway and I would keep the Tribunal and the Prosecution informed as we went along. But in the light of what I've just said and in the light of Mr. Krajisnik's comments, I should say straight away that it looks far more likely therefore that we would get some time a little while before the end of the week, we would get to that point then when I would say, well, in the light of the further work done and in the light of Mr. Krajisnik's concerns, this is as far as we can realistically go with Mr. Treanor. So if that would help as far as scheduling and as far as other witnesses are concerned. I just don't know, of course, because the details of the practical arrangements of the Prosecution are not in my hands. But, Your Honour, I hope that that's -- well, I certainly hope that's as helpful as we can be this morning in relation to this slightly unusual situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Stewart. I'd like to -- unless there's any need for the Prosecution to respond to what was just said both by Mr. Krajisnik and by Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Only with respect to one matter, Your Honour, and that is the prospect of concluding before the end of the week. Mr. Harmon and I addressed that issue specifically with Mr. Stewart earlier, because of the scheduling concerns. As a result of those discussions, we were -- and we advised the Defence accordingly, we did not schedule witnesses for this week because of the logistical difficulties involved, it would be impossible to alter that schedule at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. I'd like to make a few comments, unless there's anything to be raised at this moment, Mr. Stewart. First of all, Mr. Krajisnik, about the interpreters. Let me tell you that interpreters are human beings, although, in general, excellent human beings, doing their job very properly. Nevertheless, it can happen that a certain phrase is interpreted not fully exact. That's -- if you imagine what it takes to sit here for many hours a day and interpret every word spoken, especially if people are speaking very quickly, you'll certainly have understanding for that. If such a thing happens, especially in respect of, for example, the testimony of Mr. Treanor, we're usually dealing with texts that are already available in both languages, so it's more easy to identify any mistake in interpretation. If it's really about a critical element, if it's something of importance, as you indicated it was, then please inform Mr. Stewart, and Mr. Stewart will certainly take care that not only on paper but also if necessary in the courtroom any misunderstanding will be corrected. This same -- it was not quite clear to me what agency you are talking about, but since, in my view, it's the Registry who is finally responsible for preparing, together, of course, with the Bench, for the transcripts to be made of this hearing and about further distribution, I'm not fully aware what agency is involved. But if there's any problem in respect of that, please inform Mr. Stewart, Mr. Stewart will know how to address the Chamber, as long as it is within the responsibility of the Tribunal. Whatever happens outside, you know that all the transcripts, apart from closed and private sessions, is made available to all media agencies, whoever want to have it. What happens then with it later on, we do not know. What I do know is that sooner or later on the Internet site of the Tribunal you'll find the transcripts of open sessions, and that's the direct source for the outside world to get acquainted with what happened in this courtroom. Then finally about the funds, I'd rather not speak about it at this moment, since it's still subject for decision, although not entirely, but there are issues still to be determined. Let me just turn back to the agency. You asked the agency to see your team. I think it would be proper to do it the other way around, that if there's any complaint about whatever agency, the team will certainly find the agency you had in mind and speak with them. Then when I said that the financial issue is still to be considered, where you suggested that the Registry could provide you with a certificate about their findings, it might be that the Registry in this way would interfere in an external dispute about whether debts are still existing or not. I do not think that that's the task of the Registry, but if it is part of a decision, you can use that decision to whatever person to say that at least the Registrar or, after review, even the Chamber could not determine or could determine that a certain situation exists, and therefore in this way I think you can take advantage of decisions to be taken in this respect. Then finally, you said something about witnesses that were very much under pressure once they had been approached by the Prosecution, and you also mentioned that the Prosecution informed them that they were suspects as well. I think from the point of view of fairness to those who are giving statements to the Prosecution, it sometimes is necessary to make the potential witnesses aware that they are not beyond suspicion in certain respects. If this would keep them off from appearing as a witness, then the solution would not be not to say anything about it, but there are other ways of -- if a witness appears, there are specific rules on whether they have to fear anything at all. I couldn't guarantee to you now that a witness who appears here would never be a potential even accused in this courtroom. That's the situation. I can't change that. So therefore, it's perhaps a matter that could be discussed between Prosecution and Defence to what extent persons giving statements are unnecessarily put in a position that they are under suspicion and that would be -- would put some pressure upon them not to appear. But it's not under all circumstances unfair, and it's even under some circumstances, it's necessary to inform potential witnesses about the risks that do exist in respect of those persons themselves. So I'd rather not -- you didn't give any examples. I don't think it would be proper for the Chamber to enter into any details, but this is just a general explanation of a situation that might exist and might have caused some concern to you. Then finally, about the cross-examination. I think I do quite well understand what you intended to say, that is, that you had concerns on whether the Defence was sufficiently prepared to finish the cross-examination of Mr. Treanor. Perhaps I should better ask whether the Defence was ready to start cross-examining Mr. Treanor. The Chamber is aware of the concerns, not only expressed by you, but also by Mr. Stewart, that time for preparation might not be sufficient at this moment. I also do understand if you have worked all over the weekend on some details, that you are concerned about whether these details will properly be taken into consideration when cross-examining Mr. Treanor. I will follow the suggestion of Mr. Stewart that we start the cross-examination of Mr. Treanor now and that we'll see where we come and where the preparation seems to cause so many problems that Mr. Stewart will ask us to take a different course. I would like to leave it to that for this very moment, unless there's any urgent and necessary issue further to be raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just if I could briefly address the inference that I think was to -- that could conceivably be drawn from Mr. Krajisnik's comments, and that is that the Prosecution intentionally marshalled a team of investigators to go to the field to locate his prospective witnesses and issue warnings that would intimidate them. Of course, that is erroneous in virtually all respects, and I just want to be on the record as saying that's the case. I might add one note, and that is, of course, the Prosecution is not in possession of the Defence's witness list in the first place. Beyond that, any inferences along the lines that were suggested are flatly wrong and categorically denied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I understood the comment of Mr. Krajisnik mainly to mean that when you interview potential witnesses, that they might feel some pressure if they are informed about their potential status before this Tribunal. I did not understand it to be as an intentional attempt to intimidate witnesses. So, therefore, that's how I understood it. If I misunderstood the words of Mr. Krajisnik, I'll certainly hear either from him or from Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think -- of course, I accept and realise entirely that the Prosecution isn't in possession of some checklist of potential Defence witnesses that they can immediately go and contact. As reported to me, and these reports come from Republika Srpska, of course, there seems to be two concerns in particular. There may be others. One is that when witnesses are contacted - and this may just be a matter of practice - my information is they're told something like: We are from the United Nations and we want to talk to you about the war. If that's correct, then it would seem to us that it was rather better practice -- simply that's the report I get. If that is correct, it would be better practice, we would suggest, for it to be very clearly indicated that the investigators are from the International Criminal Tribunal for former Yugoslavia. But, Your Honour, I simply don't know in the transmission of these reports what happens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's all too vague at this moment to comment more specifically. If there are examples, if there's a real problematic situation, the Chamber would like to hear about it, because the most important thing is that whoever is needed to appear as a witness here should appear, if possible. And if you have any suggestions as far as phrasing of introducing yourself is concerned, then I'm sure that Mr. Tieger will listen to it and we'll see what he -- how he could instruct investigators to act in such a way that the purposes of this Tribunal are best served by their phrasing and while addressing potential witnesses. I think it's not an issue we should discuss at this moment in further detail. And therefore, I'd like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I respectfully agree, Your Honour. May I just mention one other point. It's only this. It is a general point again without going to specific examples, but there's just an underlying concern from the information I'm getting. It is a fine line but it's one that we suggest these investigators should be alert to that, and of course following Your Honour's observations it is only correct that anybody who might even conceivably be a potential indictee at some point should be given a warning. That's only fair. On the other hand, it's equally important that there is no exaggeration of that. So somebody who is not actually seriously ever going to be brought before this Tribunal, which is not -- I think it's fair to say is not looking to add hundreds of indictees to its work between now and certain dates in the future and is prioritising that somebody who is simply not seriously likely to -- ever to be before this Tribunal shouldn't be given the impression that they are Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. a serious prospect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I tend to agree with that. It's a matter of phrasing. It's a matter of detail. It's a matter of -- but I do agree with you that whatever is not necessary to tell a witness as far as his position is concerned at this Tribunal and that could disencourage him to give a statement or to appear as a witness in a later stage, that should be refrained. I also am aware that this is valued for both parties, as I have experienced in the past. Then, Mr. Usher, would you please escort Mr. Treanor into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Treanor. Please be seated. You'll certainly remember that at the beginning of your testimony you gave a solemn declaration. You're still bound by that solemn declaration. And although perhaps unnecessary to remind you to that I nevertheless after the long break do it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. I do remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Stewart:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, good morning again. I'd just like to clarify one or two basic points about the work that you'd done on the report. You described to the Tribunal how I think broadly speaking it's been about ten years work for you, hasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Broadly speaking, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And of course you've got a team assisting you.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In later years, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You joined the particular section of this organisation that you now work for in 1994. And up until 1994, as I understand it, you were working in the United States?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have occasion any time before 1994 to go to former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was -- well, when was your first ever visit to former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe my first visit to the former Yugoslavia was in February 1967.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during the period that we are particularly focusing on now, let me take it as, say, 1990 through to 1992, did you go to the former Yugoslavia during that three-year period?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1990 to 1992. No, I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, you said no, did you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just check, Mr. Stewart, whether there is any -- whether the translation is coming through to Mr. Krajisnik. I think there's no ... No, the translation is not ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm informed that there's a technical problem with the B/C/S translation and that we're working on it. At least, they are working on it now. Yes, Mr. Krajisnik. I do understand from your hand signal that you now receive translation again. Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: He's not, apparently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, especially in the light of the comments this morning, I really wouldn't wish to proceed without Mr. Krajisnik having translation. I'm sure Your Honour is not expecting that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not even inviting you. As soon as the technicians have solved the problem, I'd like to be informed. And if it is anticipated that it will take more than five minutes, then I'd like to be informed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The technicians have asked for a ten-minutes break, and sitting in this courtroom for ten minutes, which is the most difficult thing for a lawyer to do, is not to speak, would be overasking the parties. We'll have a break of ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. --- Break taken at 9.45 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, may I first check whether you can now hear me in a language you understand.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can, Your Honours. Thank you very much. Sorry for creating that particular problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You didn't create any problem. The problem was there. Well, Mr. Treanor will certainly have had some time to reconsider the years 1990 to 1992 and it was your last question, Mr. Stewart. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that devastating question I asked you, Mr. Treanor, you're now able to answer?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think I have the same answer I had before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Before --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm fairly confident I was not there. I have no recollection of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have any recollection -- so before that period, can you remember when is the last time you were in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the last time I was in the former Yugoslavia before I came to work at this institution was in January 1988.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you will have been back since you started to work here?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think just to clear this out of the way: You have in fact met Mr. Krajisnik, haven't you, on at least one occasion, because you participated --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- in an interview of Mr. Krajisnik, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that of course was well after the events with which this case is concerned?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever met - and first of all I'll ask this apart from any question of any interviews conducted in connection with proceedings - have you ever met any of the others, and it's rather a long list, of course, but have you met any of the other what I'll call significant players that have been dealt with in your evidence?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you mean by "significant".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's to some extent a judgement, but if we start at the top, have you ever met or had you ever met, apart from interviews conducted subsequently, had you ever met, for example, Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- Mrs. Plavsic, Mr. Koljevic? Had you ever met any of those people?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I met Ms. Plavsic within the context of an interview.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: When she arrived here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But leaving aside interviews conducted in connection with this Tribunal, you've never met any of those people?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of those people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic; you've never met him

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I met Mr. Buha.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what context?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: During a visit to Pale. I met --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's after the --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The events.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. All right. But up to, let's say, and before and up to 1992, and of course, as you've indicated to the Tribunal, you hadn't been in the former Yugoslavia for several years, you hadn't met any of the significant people or those that in your view would be significant people --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- being considered in your evidence?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- can we take it also that your -- you say that your report is not a history by any means of the conflict. Those were your words in your evidence. Is it also your approach to this report that you are not purporting to enter into the rights and wrongs in any way?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the sense that I understand that, yes. I'm not -- I do not attempt in the report to enter into any rights or wrongs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your evidence before the Tribunal before the break, you referred to the multi-party elections that took place in Slovenia, and those were on the 8th of April, 1990, and then Croatia followed soon, didn't it, on the 22nd of April. Then you said that both sets of elections resulted in severe defeats for the Communists, the League of Communists in those republics, and brought to power nationalistic parties. And then you said in both of those republics who were by no means committed to the continued existence of Yugoslavia. Now, that sounds like a bit of English understatement, Mr. Treanor. Is it not correct to say that certainly in Croatia, to say that the nationalistic parties were not committed to the continued existence of Yugoslavia as an understatement. They plainly were looking for something else, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I'd be grateful for a transcript reference numbers when counsel is making reference to particular pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I beg your pardon. Page 1264 of the transcript. And this is in the middle of the page, so it's around line 10 this passage begins.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't is true that it's not just they weren't committed to the continued existence of Yugoslavia but their policies were very clearly to gain independence?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what their policies very clearly were. They continued to participate in the process of negotiations with the other leading political factors in Yugoslavia regarding the restructuring of the state. So from that fact, I take it that they were not simply unreservably, unequivocally, committed to declaring independence or something of that sort the day they took power.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you just -- well, apart from -- after all, there's politics, isn't there, and you may not be able to come straight out and say something in absolutely trenchant terms. But in Croatia, for example, didn't it become quickly clear that the government there and Mr. Tudjman, that they were looking for an independent Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, without mastering or having in mind all the details of the developments of that period of time and the various statements and negotiations and so forth that took place, in my opinion, I think that's a fairly safe thing to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For example, by -- after all, the HDZ, which you said, and this is at page 1266 of the transcript, you informed the Tribunal that was founded in Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 18th of August, 1990, is the Croatian national party. Now, HDZ, that was exactly the same name, wasn't it, as the nationalist party in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that there were always pretty close links --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- between those two --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's fair to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- organisations? And as you told the Tribunal on the primary issue of the day, that's to say, the future of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the position of the HDZ in Bosnia-Herzegovina was that Bosnia-Herzegovina should be enabled to exercise the right of self-determination up to and including secession from Yugoslavia? That's correct, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I'm not sure whether the exact wording was the secession of Bosnia or the secession of the Croats in Bosnia, but certainly something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm actually quoting from your evidence, your description of what their policy was. And the -- you indicated yourself -- again, that was at 1266 of your transcript, and then you said, and this is at page 1270, you said that the HDZ, and talking about the BH HDZ, in August 1990, merely spoke of the right of the Croatian people to self-determination up to and including the secession of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So you expressed it just slightly differently. After all, the secession from Yugoslavia, in one case the secession of Bosnia and Herzegovina. They're entirely consistent, because we're talking of secession of Bosnia and Herzegovina from the Federation, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. But the point that I was getting back to was that they spoke of the right of the Croatian people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's clarify that. So when you talked about the HDZ speaking of the right of Croatian people up to and including secession, yes, secession of Bosnia and Herzegovina. But that's -- so piece that together for us, then. So what they -- what they -- when talking about the secession of Bosnia and Herzegovina, so they would be talking of secession of a part of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think the way that's phrased, they're talking about the whole of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's how it came across in your evidence. So that would be the effect. Clearly they only wanted it -- this is right: They only wanted it for their own purposes, for their own interests. They -- these are the Croats who wanted to associate themselves with Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, are we discussing this particular sentence or their policy in general?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, both in a sense, but let's go from the particular sentence which is after all only a lead-in, in effect, so their policy in general, yes.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Getting back to the sentence. I'll finish that. I find the wording rather peculiar. Obviously the Croatian people in Bosnia would not be able to take the whole of Bosnia and Herzegovina out of Yugoslavia. The implication there seems to be that they would agree to such a thing. On the other hand, they may have also, some of them, at least, at that time and later, advocated a partition of Bosnia and Herzegovina with part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, if we can resume calling it BH, with part of BH being a Croatian entity and perhaps joining Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm just trying to get clear what it was you were and are saying, because it was your evidence, and we're back to 1266, it was your evidence, and I'm quoting precisely, that on the primary issue of the day, that is, the future of BH, it's the HDZ in BH, its position was that BH should be enabled to exercise the right of self-determination up to and including secession from Yugoslavia. That was your evidence.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That point in their programme would -- seems to relate to the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is the reason for that that, after all, as the most -- in a sense the most obvious mechanism and the most obvious step to achieving what they wanted, which was effectively joinder with Croatia, the secession of Bosnia-Herzegovina from the Federation would be in a sense the most obvious way of achieving that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the separation of Bosnia and Herzegovina from Yugoslavia could have been seen as a step toward some other arrangement than simply an independent, integral, if I can use that expression, Bosnia-Herzegovina, including, as I mentioned just a few minutes ago, including the partition of BH with part of that republic joining Croatia. That's certainly one of the options that was on the table. But when precisely and to what extent that in fact became the policy of the HDZ is another issue. There were differences of opinion within the HDZ, both in -- as far as I'm aware of, both in Croatia and in Bosnia, as to the best policy to follow in that connection. There were people that were in favour of partitioning BH and joining part of it to Croatia, and there were those that were against doing that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, is the position this, that for those within the HDZ who were looking to join a part of BH with Croatia, that the more promising way of doing that, if you like, was to create a more general breakup, a more generally fluid situation with BH seceding from the Federation. It was more likely then that in the fallout from that exercise they would be able to achieve what they wanted. Is that a fair --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I think I said a few minutes ago, that could be seen by certain people as a step in that direction, undoubtedly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your evidence earlier, and this was page 1265 of the transcript, you talked about the various amendments to the BH constitution, and in particular, Amendment 62, saying that -- specifying the territory of BH was indivisible and the boundaries of the republic could only be changed at a referendum of the citizens with a two thirds majority. Now, there's an issue as to whether that was -- in effect, that was the internal boundaries, I think you indicated, that that amendment had in mind.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think by boundaries they're referring to the external boundaries of the republic. I mean, it doesn't have any other boundaries as a republic. If by internal boundaries you mean the boundaries of the municipalities or something, I don't think that's what's in question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, thank you for that clarification, then. Now, one of the things that you --- I think you were at pains to indicate in your evidence is that, Mr. Treanor, you're not a lawyer and you haven't had legal training?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think you indicated you don't really wish and are not equipped to enter into discussion or debate about the legal aspects of these matters.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we look at binder 1, I hope you have your various binders there available to you over there, I think, aren't they? Are those Mr. Treanor's copies there?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, those are the, to the best of my knowledge, the Registry's binders and not Mr. Treanor's, and he had with him during direct examination a different set consisting, as I recall, primarily of B/C/S documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's work on the basis of the documents that have been admitted into evidence, which are at this moment in the hands of the registrar. I've got my own copy with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Fine. As long as of course the Tribunal has its own copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It would be -- Mr. Stewart, this morning, I guessed that you would start at 1 and not at 18, so I took the first four. If you could give us an indication what binders to bring for the next session, then it would certainly help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I can certainly say that as far as the whole day is concerned, we won't get beyond, say, number 8. But I think for the first couple of sessions, Your Honours would be fairly safe with, I think, 1 to 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We've got one copy now and at the next break I think we could bring some more copies. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, the -- we looked at tab 2, which is -- I hope you don't feel handicapped by having to look at it in English.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would feel a bit handicapped looking at it in English, but the B/C/S seems to be in here as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, well, that's good, then. It's the programme, then, of the Serbian Democratic Party. I just want to clarify with you: Would you agree there's absolutely nothing surprising at all in this programme?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, without trying to put too fine a point on the meaning of "surprising", I find the programme rather unexceptionable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, frankly, it's pretty anodyne, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be qualified that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, would you qualify it as that way?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably not. I mean, "anodyne" is not a word I use very frequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not only that Mr. Treanor might not use it very frequently, but for us for understanding, the word is not -- it looks as if it comes from chemistry, more or less, anodyne.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think -- I beg your pardon. I think harmless would do as a word. Harmless, bland.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I described it as being rather unremarkable, and I'll stick with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's not a bad word. It's your word and you're the witness, Mr. Treanor. So it's unremarkable. After all, it's, well, random in a way, but equality is the basis of joint life and democratic Yugoslavia structured as a modern federal state. It's all status quo stuff as far as that's concerned, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It does contain, doesn't it, a bit of, if you like, historical reference to what the Serbs, with justification, regard as terrible times, in connection with the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Ustasha, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But apart from those significant historical references, unremarkable is your word?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's clearly a -- the programme of a Serbian party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you -- then you went on to tab 4, same bundle, and we looked at the statute of the SDS, and you drew attention to Article 9. And I'm going on the point, this is at page 1271 of the transcript, particular point to which you drew attention, that the rights and obligations of SDS BH members are, and then you listed them all, and then you said: So party discipline -- well, you drew attention to obligation to obey party regulations and support the achievement of its goals and programme orientation and then you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down for the benefit of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... something that was required and -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The interpreters ask you to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: More than one person has asked me to slow down, so I will try to do that immediately, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Article 9, yes, you drew attention to that article and then specifically to the provision about obeying party regulations. And I'm really just wondering. You say party discipline was something that was required and expected. And I don't mean this rudely at all, Mr. Treanor, but is that any more than a statement of the blindingly obvious for a political party?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how the statutes in this respect of political parties across the world or Europe read in this respect. The thing that I found interesting in that is that that is the type of party discipline that was required in Communist parties and in -- I believe in the League of Communists, a rather top-down approach to things. Once decisions had Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. been made, then people were obliged to adhere to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And then you addressed briefly, page 1271 of the transcript, the central organs of the party, the party assembly. Now, that was originally limited to a thousand, wasn't it, and then the maximum number was reduced by Amendment 300, wasn't it? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought it was 200. I don't recall the exact provisions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think it was 300, actually, but we probably don't need to quibble. Article 13 at tab 4, the Assembly comprises all members of the party until its membership exceeds 1.000. And then you refer to the party president and the Main Board and the Executive Committee. We'll come back to some of these organs in more detail in due course. But you said yourself in your evidence at that point that the Main Board and the Executive Committee were less important. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Less important than what?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, less important than the other two, the party assembly and the party president.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to the statute, the Assembly was the -- certainly the supreme organ, and certainly the Executive Board was less important than that, and the Main Board was less important than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll look at these in more detail. But perhaps we can get it straight, because they're perhaps two entirely different things. As far as the formal structure is concerned, the Assembly was the supreme body; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a practical matter, do you say that the Assembly was an unwieldy body that didn't in fact truly take the decisions, or that it did truly take the decisions?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it only met once a year, and the types of things that it considered were rather broad. For instance, the statute and the programme carrying out elections to the various party organs seemed to be the main activity of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So the -- in your evidence, what seems to emerge is that then that the Assembly, for the reasons you've indicated, it may be technically the supreme body but it doesn't meet very often, it's quite a large body, the effective decisions have really got to be taken somewhere else, haven't they?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I think that was the reason for the creation of the Main Board.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you yourself, when you say the Main Board and the Executive Committee are less important, your evidence appeared to be, is this right, that the Main Board wasn't all that important in practice either?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You -- I think you've hit the nail right on the head there. If you read the statute, the Main Board comes out to be -- seems to be very important indeed, but as we look at the documentation that's available to us, we can see that the Main Board really didn't meet all that frequently and did not have very many formal sessions where it was strictly a meeting of the Main Board and made the type of decisions that seem to be foreseen in the statute. So in practice, it did not operate in the manner and at the level of importance that one would gather simply by reading the statute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And the Executive Board, that applies even more so, doesn't it, the Executive Board fed in to the Main Board, but it also wasn't really a central decision-making organ?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Executive Board, according to the statute, had a different function than the Main Board. However, we do see that the Executive Board, at least after the 1991 party assembly, when the party organs were reconstituted, we see the Executive Board meeting on a fairly regular basis and dealing with the types of issues that it's supposed to deal with, and it became a -- apparently became a fairly efficient organ of the party, along the lines that one would expect by reading the statute. But it was not supposed to be a policy-making body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just interfere. When you're talking about the Executive Board, you're referring to the Executive Committee, I take it, as it appears in this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I think the -- as often happens with the translation, I think the terminology changes quite frequently within the documentation and indeed within the evidence. It is -- it's often referred to as Executive Board, often referred to as Executive Committee. It's exactly the same organ, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's right, Mr. Treanor, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I believe in our report and in my testimony hopefully we used the terms Executive Board and Main Board.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you do in fact at paragraph 42 of your report, you do say the Executive Board was an important forum for decision making in its own right.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's what you've just described. And I suppose that, is this right, that part of the reason for that is a very simple one, that it was smaller than the Main Board, which was in turn smaller than the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it certainly was smaller.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Krajisnik was never a member of that, was he?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Executive Committee -- the Executive Board, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There are a number of different organs. I'd like to go quickly through a list at this point, really perhaps just to put some of them on one side so we don't have to be troubled with them, and then can focus perhaps in due course on those that are important. The -- there's a body called the Council for the Protection of the Constitutional Order. Are you familiar with that, as an organ?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Presidency of...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, does that mean anything to you? I appreciate these are all translations, but it's translated as Council for the Protection of the Constitutional Order. Do you know anything about that? Mrs. Plavsic was the chairman.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's a council operating within the framework of the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of BH.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't the position this: It was previously that before the elections and before the formation of the new parties, that had previously been a BH body, there had been a BH body as opposed to an SDS body, the SDS didn't exist, Council for the Protection of the Constitutional Order, that's correct, is it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe it existed prior to 1990.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could both speakers kindly remember to pause between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, there's a very important message on page 32, line 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For all of us. You're even violating when I said it was an important message. I do not mind from a personal point of view, but you spoke at the same time when I said this, and it's impossible for the transcribers to put everything on the record if two persons are speaking at the same time or are interrupting each other. So could we not only not interrupt each other, but at the same time take a little pause between question and answer, and answer and question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Certainly. I apologise. I'm sure Your Honour understands no discourtesy was intended. I was intending to acknowledge that I had just seen that message, and I apologise if it appeared otherwise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, so the -- that previous BH body, what happened was this, wasn't it, that after the elections, then, each party set up its own, the SDS, the SDA, and the HDZ, set up its own equivalent Council for the Protection of the Constitutional Order?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not aware that that's the case. The council that I referred to, that I believe existed prior to the 1990 elections continued to exist within the BH Presidency after those elections. That's the only body of that name that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, since there appears to be a difference between the information that I'm putting to you and what you're saying, perhaps we can short-circuit it by asking whether in your view it's important anyway in the context of your report and the issues with which we're concerned in this case.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the importance of that body is similar to the importance of other offices that SDS appointees, if I can use that expression, meaning people that were put forward for a particular position, whether it be in the election or in a more pointed process after the election, gave the SDS, as it would have given the other political parties and the positions they held, access to official information and the ability to influence official action. The particular council we're referring to was chaired by Dr. Plavsic, who was an SDS candidate for that -- to the Presidency and was successful, and within the framework of the work of the Presidency, they had different councils and committees, that sort of thing. And the different members of the Presidency were allotted chairmanships or memberships on various of those bodies, which also included other officials, such as ministers. That particular body dealt with matters related to the Ministry of Internal Affairs. So that gave Dr. Plavsic an important insight into what was going on in the Ministry of Internal Affairs and the ability to influence developments there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was -- concerned internal security issues?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's right, isn't it, Mr. Krajisnik was not involved at all with that body?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not a member of that body, no. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll rephrase it as two separate questions, then. First of all, as you've just confirmed, he wasn't ever a member of that body?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you aware of his ever having had any involvement with that body?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure what you mean by "involvement". I do not have the minutes of all the meetings of that body that took place, on the one hand; on the other, there are many telephone conversations in which issues surrounding -- issues that would have been within the purview of that body that were discussed, and I believe he participated in some of those discussions. I can't think of a particular one offhand, but I'm trying to be cautious in my answer. So as far as involvement is concerned, that's about all I can say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Treanor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm looking at the clock. If you could find a suitable moment within the next three to four minutes to have a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Certainly. I can do exactly that. But Your Honour would like me to use up another three or four minutes preferably?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then we'll have a break of 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, I certainly wouldn't be fair to you, I'm certainly not trying to push you into, if you like, proving a negative or some assertion that he never had any involvement, because you can't know that. I think that's what you're implying. So what I'm inviting you to do is to point specifically positively to anything in your report and anything that you can identify now which shows specific contacts or work by Mr. Krajisnik with that particular organ, the Council for the Protection of the Constitutional Order.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of anything of the nature you seem to be describing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that would, I think, be as convenient a point as any, I hope, for the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll then have a break until five minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, we had been looking at the Council for the Protection of the Constitutional Order, but we can leave that. And there are a number of bodies we'll come back to which plainly, in your view, as you've expressed it, are important, the Deputies' Club. So I'll put it on one side, not because it's unimportant, but because it is important. The Economic Council. That was a body of which Mr. Krajisnik, who is an economist by training, was a member, but you wouldn't suggest that the Economic Council is material for the purposes of this case, would you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I'm aware, we don't have any significant documentation relating to that council. There are references to it in some of the documents that I presented in my testimony, where that council was assigned certain tasks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All I'm getting at --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I'm thinking of the question of the meeting about landownership or land use. But absent documentation from that body, I can't say how important it in fact was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll, as I did earlier, I'll put it in a slightly different way, then. Mr. Treanor, on what you know and everything you've read, you're not able, are you, to suggest that the work of the Economic Council has any real significance for this case?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm certainly unable to say on the basis of the documentation that I've seen that it was a very important body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it's clearly important for the economy, but apart from that. You say you can't say it's very important. Indicate whether it really has any importance at all for this case, in your view.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of the documentation that I've seen, I certainly would not say that it's a very important body, or even perhaps an important body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The expanded Presidency again I'll put on one side, because clearly on your evidence that's more central. The -- similarly with the National Security Council. An organisation, the personnel and organisation committee, or an organ, personnel and organisation committee which you had mentioned, you described it in your report, and I'm now talking about the initial printed report, as a potentially -- another potentially important body. But it's -- and Mr. Krajisnik was a member of that body. But it's again, I'd suggest to you, say if you disagree, that for the purposes of this case and the issues in this case, with which you are, after all, pretty familiar, Mr. Treanor, personnel and organisation committee is again not particularly important, is it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure what the issues are in this case and all the legal ramifications. But let me just say in relation to that particular body, the situation there is similar to that with the Economic Council in that I'm not aware that we have much documentation relating to its activities. We do have a few documents, which I think is probably a few more than we have relating to the Economic Council. However, those documents indicate that is seems to have had the function typical for such bodies, again going back to the Communist period, of identifying the, in this case the SDS candidates for various posts that the party wishes to endorse for various government positions. So if I'm being asked how important do I think that body is, I think it, in and of itself within the framework of the party's operations, was an important body. We just don't have much documentation relating to its operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. What I'm suggesting really, Mr. Treanor, is we don't operate in some sort of a vacuum. You're an expert witness, but you do, after all, know very well, don't you, what the charges are against Mr. Krajisnik and what the essential thrust of the Prosecution's case against him is?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have -- I certainly have an idea, yes. I mean, I -- again, not being a lawyer, I don't know whether I could put it in the proper terms, but certainly I have an idea of what the charges are, and if I understand your question correctly, the -- I would say that the -- this particular body does not play the role that other bodies do, for instance, the expanded Presidency, certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But in fact the gap is really rather bigger, that there are two separate things, aren't they. There's a body that was important in the overall functioning of the SDS and the government generally at that time, but which is nevertheless clearly not at all important in relation to the issues which this Prosecution of Mr. Krajisnik is concerned and that this particular body, the personnel and organisation committee, is exactly in that category.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it may be or it may not be. I'm -- have not written the report to make a case but simply to set out the documents as we know them relating to the SDS and its various party organs and the other bodies that it created and how they operated. Whether something is important within the framework of this case or not is not really for me to say. I wouldn't have thought it was, if you want an opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, your report, after all, this report that's been produced and refined over many years, again it hasn't been produced in a vacuum. It's been produced by you working for the OTP, for this Tribunal, hasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's not an academic study of the -- it may include that, but it's not primarily an academic study of the situation in Bosnia for professors around the world to read. It's for this Tribunal, for prosecutions of alleged, to use a broad term, war criminals.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you ask me to characterise the report, I would feel quite comfortable in characterising it as an academic study for this institution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but what this institution does is prosecute and judge and either convict or acquit people accused of broadly war crimes, doesn't it? That's what it does?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what certain people in this institution do, namely, the Trial Chamber. It's not my function.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's just that you do, in the course of your evidence and in your report, you have very clearly identified certain organs as important or very important, haven't you, such as the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's fair to say, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My apologies for --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- talking at the same moment as you. But you seem to be strangely reluctant, although you classify or characterise certain organs as very important or important, you seem strangely reluctant to downgrade any of them by saying they're not important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't want to intercede, but this line of questioning seems to ignore the testimony of the witness that this particular body was important within the framework of the party's operations. It would seem to me that Mr. Stewart received an answer to the question he posed and is now engaged in a debate about a preparatory matter that preceded that response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I understood the testimony of the witness until now, and I add this before giving you an opportunity to respond to what Mr. Tieger said, is that on the basis of the documentation he studied that he could identify certain bodies as -- of importance for this case with his knowledge but it seems that the witness is reluctant and I think correctly so, to say that something is not important because he has no overall overview of the case as a whole. Not working in the vacuum does not mean that you have a hundred per cent knowledge of whatever could come up in a case. So therefore, I'd like you to move on. If you'd like to put a final question on this subject, it's fine, but it's of no use to continue for another 20 minutes to see how you'd like to hear from the witness that a certain part is not important and where the witness seems to be hesitant to express himself clearly on the non-importance of a certain body where he has no full knowledge. That's how I understand his repeated reference to the documents he studied from the basis of what he saw. So please, would you keep this in mind and then proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: With the same vein -- thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the same vein, Mr. Treanor, can I ask you, then, about the Political Council. And in your report, and I'm talking about the actual report rather than your evidence, at paragraph 39, and I'm citing, you say: The Political Council in which Plavsic and Krajisnik sometimes participated played an important advisory role in practice. And then in paragraph 40, the following paragraph, you say: The Political Council played a subsidiary advisory role while other statutory bodies did not make significant contributions. So you see, Mr. Treanor, what I'm just trying to get us to focus on what's really important. So as far as the Political Council is concerned, in the light of those two comments which do appear to be marginally different, at least in tone, where do you place the Political Council in importance for what you know about this case?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, I can only place the Political Council within the framework of the activities of the SDS, and on the basis of the documentation which we dispose of, I would say that the Political Council was a -- was an important forum of discussion. It included many prominent Serbs, and it seems to have been called upon quite frequently, when I say it seems to have, because we have frequent references to its meetings, but perhaps not all the references. And it -- the people in the council offered opinions on important subjects of the day and the council as a whole discussed important subjects of the day. So it was one of the important bodies on which the leadership of the SDS drew for advice and consultation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the Statutes Council, which is mentioned at page 38 of your report, the Statutes Council, Mr. Treanor, could we put that one safely in the category of clearly unimportant for the purposes of this case?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, I can only speak to what its role appears to have been within the SDS, which -- about which we don't have terribly much documentation. So it does not appear to have played a very important role within the SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The supervisory board, you say that in practice its activities were related to auditing the party's financial activities and informing the competent organs of its findings. Now, I'm not suggesting money is not important but can we also safely put the supervisory board in the box labelled not important for this case?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, I don't know what may or may not be important for this case. You said money is important. Maybe money is important for this case. But in relation to this body, we seem to have more references to it and that sort of thing. But perhaps as a rule of thumb I could say that the amount of space devoted in the report to a given body is a fair indication of how important I think it was within the operations of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, if I may give you some guidance. Whenever this issue of important or not of a body comes up again, could you please ask the witness whether this body belongs to the category he did not identify on the basis of his studies.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, Your Honour. Sorry. I didn't catch that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
