utterances.text: He did not identify on the basis of his studies of importance. That's another way of saying almost the same. But that prevents -- that Mr. Treanor has to explain again and again within what limits he gives his opinion and could save you some time. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- in fact, Mr. Treanor, really, I've pretty much gotten to the end of that checklist. It's the way it sometimes happens. The -- page 1283 of the transcript of your evidence, you talked about the amendments to the constitution, the BH constitution, and that within the Assembly, there would be a commission for the question of the equality of peoples. Perhaps you could expand a little on what you understand the functions of that particular commission to have been.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in my understanding, the functions of that commission would have been akin to the -- that of the chambers of nationalities, I think they were called, chambers of peoples that the SDS had suggested creating in the autumn of 1990, and I'm referring to Dr. Karadzic's letter to the then existing Assembly of BH. That is, it would have had the function of considering matters that were important to the national rights of the various peoples within BH, especially the constituent peoples, and would have had to approve any measures that affected those rights.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the letter that you just referred to, to get clear, that's the letter, isn't it, at tab 9 of the first bundle? I think you still have that file, don't you, number 1, in front of you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the letter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the one you're talking about. And you said in your evidence, and this is at page 1287 of the transcript, that -- well, just before that, actually, you commented. You said that one of the -- you said the force of the act of the amendment which Dr. Karadzic sought would basically have given any one of the three constituent nations of BH a veto over any measure before the Assembly which it felt adversely affected its interests as a nation. And then you said: In other words, it would have been impossible for -- under this proposed arrangement for the Serbian deputies in that council to block the secession of BH from Yugoslavia. Of course it follows it also naturally would have been possible for the Muslim deputies to block in the same way. That follows, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And perhaps in theory the Croat?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- deputies. And then you say that not surprisingly, and this is at page 1287, you say: Not surprisingly this letter did not draw favourable action given that the Assembly was on its way out. I wonder if you could clarify. What's the connection between the fact that the Assembly was on its way out and the lack of any favourable action or reaction to his letter?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's -- I've made a presumption, perhaps unwarranted, but I thought obvious that given that this letter was dated the 8th of October, 1990 and that elections had been scheduled two months before, the elections due to take place the following month, that the Assembly whose term in office was obviously very limited in time at this particular date, was hardly likely to take action to amend the constitution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it's a bit more than that, isn't it? Isn't it not just that the Assembly was on its way out. The timing might not have been perfect from the, if you like, the practical point of view, for everybody to make those amendments. The lack of any favourable reaction was that the recipients within the Muslim deputies and Croat deputies just didn't want such an amendment; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you say the Muslim deputies and the Croatian deputies, we're talking about an assembly now that was elected during the Communist period. So --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, yes, but, Mr. Treanor, within that assembly, is it not correct that for practical purposes, any individual deputy would have been likely to have identified himself or herself with Serb, Muslim, or Croat nation or community?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the ethnic composition of that assembly, but there were undoubtedly many Muslims and Croats, as well as Serbs, in that assembly, and there were also undoubtedly many people who identified themselves as being Yugoslavs and members of other nations. As far as the political aspects of the question is concerned, I would presume, and I don't think that's what I was thinking of when I gave that answer, that the position of the Assembly would have been -- well, we've already made our provisions in that respect in the amendment that I referred to, and that's as far as we're going to go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. It's just that the two reasons -- in fact, you gave two reasons in your evidence, this is at 1287 of the transcript. You said not surprisingly, this letter did not draw favourable action, given that the Assembly was on its way out, the point we just mentioned, and perhaps given the fact that the letter confused Amendment 60 with Amendment 70. But giving those two reasons, I'm suggesting that rather glosses over the much more simple, fundamental reason which was that a very significant number of the recipients of this letter simply were opposed to any such change.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they may have been, but I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know the reason was that the letter confused Amendment 60 with Amendment 70, but you are content to offer it as a suggested reason, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's something -- that is something which, like the date of the letter, proceeds from the letter itself. I would say that the letter has drafting problems and the date of the letter is important in connection with the fact that that Assembly was no longer going to be in office very long. If they had been of a mind to make such changes, that presumably would have taken some length of time anyways. How long, I don't know, but I just think -- my -- the thrust of my answer was that from the technical point of view, it was rather late in the day to suggest that this Assembly make such changes. Now, they had, in the constitutional amendment the you referred to initially, made some provisions in that regard, and as I say, they quite likely would have felt, since they're the ones that instituted it, that that's how they dealt with that problem and that was -- the way they wanted to deal with it and not consider something else offered by someone who kind of confused the various amendments of the constitution, doesn't seem to know what he's talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you -- in your evidence, and this was at page 1287 still at the transcript, you referred to an open-air meeting in Banja Luka on the 13th of October, 1990. Do you remember that? And a speech by Mr. Karadzic. And then we saw a video of that speech, actually. And you said, and this is at page 1289 of the transcript, that: We hear Dr. Karadzic specifically addressing the situation in Croatia. He said that if the Croats in Croatia wanted to leave Yugoslavia, that's fine, but they can't take the Serbs in Croatia with them. And that's in the area of Krajina; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Primarily.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Primarily. And then he moved on to address the situation in BH. This is you talking now: Then he, Dr. Karadzic, moved on to address the situation in BH and raising the fear that the next step would be to try to take BH in its entirety, including the Serbs, in it outside of Yugoslavia. Well, first of all, he was right, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That that materialised, indeed, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there was, from what you know of the situation at the time, it isn't just that he was proved right, as it happens, but it was the very next day, if he was proved right, that did materialise, but there was every justification at that time for that fear, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure what you mean by every justification.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll rephrase it. It was an entirely reasonable view for a political leader to take at that time and to express.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From his point of view, definitely, to be on guard for such a contingency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, in his position, it would have been rather irresponsible or remiss of him not to recognise that risk, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I think I indicated, that this was the burning issue of the day, I think is the expression I used. The future of the relationship between BH and the rest of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you referred yourself - this is at the foot of 1289 of your evidence. You say reference is also made to Assembly decisions which could appear legitimate, the majority of the Assembly could vote for the secession of BH, and all of the Serbian delegates would be against that. But since they wouldn't have a majority, this would look perfectly legitimate to the outside world and this is what they were determined to prevent. So what in effect, without getting into any legal technicalities about it, Mr. Treanor, this was a fear of what can sometimes be referred to as the tyranny of the majority, if you like, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's fair to say that's very much what they were afraid of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your evidence at page 1292, we looked at, or you looked at and drew the court's attention to tab 11 in this same bundle. When I say "bundle", I'm afraid I'm just slipping into English terminology all the time. I'm referring to a file. When I say bundle 1, I really always mean just file 1. What you say, you drew the Court's attention to it. You say, in the second paragraph, according to this decision -- according to the decision of the Serbian National Council of BH, the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina shall not recognise any decision to change the state character of BH taken by the deputies rather than the people, but only a decision reached through a referendum of the Serbian people. And then the way you describe that, you say: So here the Serbian National Council is basically announcing, it is in effect setting itself up as a Serbian Chamber of Peoples, which Dr. Karadzic had earlier sought, and giving themselves a veto, so to speak, over any decisions made by the Assembly that would affect the interests of the Serbian people. Now, I just want to clarify with you: That's the way you expressed it in your evidence, giving themselves a veto over any decisions made by the Assembly that would affect the interests of the Serbian people, that's -- if you reconsider that, that's too broadly expressed, isn't it, Mr. Treanor?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this decision makes reference to the change in the state character of BH. I was trying to link this -- the setting up of this council with the previous demands for a chamber made in the October letter, which would have had a broader mandate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But what you were specifically talking about in your evidence is what the Serbian National Council was announcing and what it was announcing and also what they were giving themselves by -- that was your phrase, giving themselves by this declaration. It was very specifically confined to changes of the state character of BH, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says here, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then when we go on to what you said, and this is at page 1295, the reference of your -- the transcript of your evidence. You were referring to the interview which is at tab 13 in the same bundle. And working from the translation, the relevant paragraph is the one at the top of the last page of the English translation. It's probably the last page of the B/C/S as well. The paragraph that begins in English: Serbian priorities. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Serbian --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, in translation, of course. Serbian priorities are the preservation of the spiritual, cultural, political and state unity of the Serbian people. A Serbian priority is the return of the Serbian people among the happy peoples and the Serbian state among the happy states. A Serbian priority is preventing a single Serbian village from being left out of Yugoslavia and remaining in some new Independent State of Croatia which existed during the Second World War. It says "NDH" in the English translation. Is that a historical term?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's an acronym for the B/C/S word for Independent State of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. And then you -- what you said in your evidence, this is at page 1295 of the transcript, you said -- having read that passage, you said: So here he seems, and this is Dr. Karadzic, he seems to be claiming for Yugoslavia every Serbian village in Bosnia. But he's not saying that, is he? This is relating specifically and only to those villages which could fall into Croatia.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that statement is -- relates to the situation in Croatia, undoubtedly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. So what I mean is, what I'm putting to you is, where you said he seems to be claiming for Yugoslavia every Serbian village in Bosnia, he's not making any such claim here, because this doesn't relate to the whole of Bosnia, does it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it seems to me that mutatis mutandis he would have made the same claim for Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mutatis mutandis?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But he's not making it here.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This statement directly relates to -- or mentions specifically Croatia, but he's talking about Serbian priorities and being opposed to a single Serbian village being left out of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And remaining in some new Independent State of Croatia. So it doesn't -- he's not possibly talking about those which are so far away from Croatia that nobody would seriously suggest, at least of all the Croats, fall into that independent state; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. Could you repeat that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because he's specifically talking -- after all, let's start at the beginning. Croatia was a real crisis at this time, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact -- although there were, of course, these concerns by Dr. Karadzic and others about where the future of BH was going, there was an immediate problem and conflict, wasn't there, involving Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that's what he's talking about. And he's talking about here only about those villages which are, my phrase here, for the purpose of the question, vulnerable to being absorbed into Croatia at some point?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: He makes reference to preventing a single Serbian village. Now, it seems to me that that remark betrays -- or indicates an attitude that was easily transferrable to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I won't pursue this point any further now, Mr. Treanor. Can we move on, then, in the same bundle, the same file, to letters -- well, letter 14. It's a letter from Dr. Karadzic to Mr. Milosevic. And you read this letter, or the two paragraphs of it, anyway, the paragraphs beginning: Your election means. And also: Through your electoral victory. You read those out to the Trial Chamber when you gave your evidence. What I'm wondering and asking you, Mr. Treanor, is: What the letter -- you drew attention to it and you read it out -- what it actually adds to anything. What do you suggest is its significance?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps you can give me a tab number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. Did I not give it? Tab 14. I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: 14. Okay. Well, I find this letter interesting in that, on the one hand, not surprisingly, it indicates on the part of Dr. Karadzic a not surprising favourable attitude and support toward the authorities in Serbia. I think, as we've been discussing, one of the primary goals of Dr. Karadzic's party was that the Serbs in Bosnia remain in the same state with Serbia. On the other hand, it's a letter of support to someone who, at least until very recently, when they changed the name, at least, if not the structure, of the ruling party in Serbia, support for someone who had been a lifelong Communist, which is something that Dr. Karadzic and his party were opposed to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what is the -- is that the point of interest in the letter?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those two things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what do you say? There's an irony in that or it's some contradictory element, or what?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, his expression of support extends to, as I put it, the Communist rulers of Serbia, from whom, since they had won the election, he may have hoped to get some support for his position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's just this, isn't it, that you work with the people you have to work with, and if they -- somebody gets elected to power somewhere else, then -- well, I'll put it more broadly, Mr. Treanor. All over the world, politicians write congratulatory letters to each other upon their election, sometimes through gritted teeth, sometimes with enthusiasm?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that may be the case. That may be his motivation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what it looks like, doesn't it? It's a -- if you like, it's a bread-and-butter letter written by one political leader to another, knowing that he's won a very comfortable election victory and he's the person he's going to have to deal with?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he wrote the letter, so there's obviously an explanation for it, and I would agree with you that that's it. But there are other courses of action he could have taken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What, such as -- a disparaging letter and then spoiling relations for ever more? Something like that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could have refrained from writing any letter at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tab 15, if you'd turn over, is not an election in the same way, but same sort of spirit really, isn't it? It's a congratulatory letter. And of course it involves perfectly natural support for the Serb people in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, this letter is certainly less surprising, but it does embody the solidarity which Dr. Karadzic felt for the Serbs in Krajina who, by the way, had a ruling party with the same name as his and a party which he, I believe it's correct to say, tended to view as sort of their older sister in certain respects.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That reminds me, actually. There was an entirely different question I just wanted to ask you at some point. Now, as it happens, Mr. Krajisnik's own name as an origin of the name indicates, doesn't it, it signifies somebody from the Krajina, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Krajisnik. I just wanted to ask you this specifically, because occasionally, and it may help the Tribunal, occasionally, the word "Krajisnik" appears in a document, and it's not referring to Mr. Krajisnik at all, is it; it's making a reference to somebody from Krajina in more general terms?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And there are two Krajinas. A Croatian Krajina and a Bosnian Krajina. And the word does appear in documents in the sense of someone from Krajina, one of the Krajinas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's only this, Mr. Treanor, one has to be a tiny bit careful when "Krajisnik" leaps off the page, to be sure that it is in fact Mr. Krajisnik who is being referred to as opposed to this other use of the word?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The -- so anyway, you -- this was at 1297 of the transcript. After all, you, Mr. Treanor, in your chronological survey for the Tribunal, you picked out this letter at tab 15 to Mr. Babic, to Mr. Milan Babic as worth specific mention and worth citing to the Tribunal particular paragraphs. So I just wanted to be clear. You say: In summary we have an expression in that letter of solidarity with the Croatian Serbs, who had the same desire as expressed by the leaders of the SDS that the Serbs in Croatia should remain within Yugoslavia. I just invite you to confirm that there's absolutely nothing surprising about that. It's exactly what you would expect and it was in the context of the time an entirely reasonable and legitimate political position to adopt?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's what you'd expect from Dr. Karadzic, certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it's not only what you'd expect from Dr. Karadzic, is it? Mr. Treanor, you've been working in relation to this region and have written this very extensive academic report. It was an entirely reasonable political stance for Dr. Karadzic to adopt, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: For Dr. Karadzic, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think the head of the HDZ in Bosnia would send such a letter. I mean, so from Dr. Karadzic's political perspective, and we've seen that in the documents I've presented, beginning with the party programme, this is indeed perfectly natural.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's perhaps my fault. I'm not putting the question well enough, Mr. Treanor. The -- you say it's reasonable from Dr. Karadzic's own perspective. Well, no doubt among other things he saw it that way. Given that this was a pluralist society, especially after those elections, you had Muslims, you had Croats, you had Serbs, that any reasonably objective political observer would have said: Well, all right. I understand what the Muslims are saying, I understand what the Croats are saying, I understand what Dr. Karadzic is saying as a Serb. And that looks like perfectly reasonable politics to me.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the SDS, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- you referred to the composition of the chamber, then, after the elections in November 1990, and you gave the figures, and you illustrated how it was the numbers, as it often is in politics, which created the difficulty. The -- you gave some figures - this is at page 1299 of the transcript - that the SDS won a total of 72 seats, 38 seats in the Chamber of Municipalities, and 34 seats in the Chamber of Citizens. So that was how the 72 was made up. But the SDA had won a total of 86 seats, and the HDZ, you thought, 44. And then you said those two chambers are composed of on the one hand the 130 deputies in the Chamber of Citizens and 110 in the Chamber of Municipalities. And then you said the total of 230 is important. Mr. Treanor, this is a rather nit-pickingly small point in a sense, but you refer to 130 deputies in the Chamber of Citizens, 110 in the Chamber of Municipalities, and then a total of 230. In fact, they total 240. I just wonder whether you're in a position today to confirm which of those figures is the one that needs correcting.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I confess. I have a hard time keeping that straight. I believe it's 110 and 120.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So it's probably -- well, we'll check that, then, is the easiest thing to do.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's all right. It's probably the 120 that needs correcting.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know it's 110 for the one chamber.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The arithmetic obviously needs adjusting somewhere, or the figures. But the 230 to 240, I wanted to try and get it straight, is not critical, is it, because the same problem about the Serb deputies being below the necessary threshold to block a change arises whether it's 230 or 240 anyway, doesn't it so...

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The point that I was alluding to is the fact that they did get together as a single group on many occasions and decide as a unified body and not as separate chambers. So the total strength in the two chambers becomes important per se.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, if we look at tab 16, please. This is the diary or translation of the diary of Mr. Maksimovic. I'm never quite sure. Where does the emphasis come in the syllables, Mr. Treanor?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm never quite sure either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, that makes two of us.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maksimovic is fine with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. Would Your Honour give me a moment. Sometimes the transcript has -- you have to go back quite a long way in the transcript to pick up the page number of the document that you're referring to. In the -- my apologies, Your Honour. It's page 3. I beg your pardon. It's page 3 of the translation. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Towards the top it says -- the second -- what's described in your evidence, this is at page 1304 of the transcript, the second bullet point: What have our first parliamentary experiences shown regarding our national protection? You see that point. Then you say -- well, you cite the next bit of the document. We will have heavy fighting and so on. And then you say -- this is in your evidence at 1305: There are two points which I would remind the Court came up in our discussion of the programme of the SDS and Dr. Karadzic's speech. The feeling that the municipal boundaries should perhaps be redrawn and the desire, as we saw later expressed, to form a Chamber of nationalities to prevent outvoting. Then you say: Move down a little bit, in the middle of the page, the present state of our unity - and we see that in the middle of page 3 of the translation. The present state of our unity is unsufficient [sic]. We've heard many promises at meetings but what have we done? The unity of Serbian deputies has not been shaped. Some believe that the intellectual level of our deputies is satisfactory. However, our position in parliament will never be favourable. I am certain of that. There will be all sorts of things in the Assembly, outvoting, treachery, rows, walkouts and protests. Is that democracy? We'll see. So again we have the fear of outvoting in the Assembly. It's really -- it's a rather long preamble, Mr. Treanor, to the question, but again, you felt it valuable to draw attention specifically to what appeared in this diary at this point, but is the fundamental point about forming a Chamber of Nationalities to prevent outvoting, do you see that as, in substance, the same as the proposals which have been put forward by Dr. Karadzic in his earlier speeches and letter?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'd say it's the same idea. There are no specifics here, but it's obviously designed to meet the same situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The mechanics changed, but the underlying point is the same. There's just a --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- if you like, a repeated attempt to deal with this obvious problem of potential outvoting in the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The otherwise, is there -- you cited this -- these fairly extensive passages from that diary. What particular significance, if any, do you attach to those cited passages?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Where are we now?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's the present state of our -- well, the particular passage which you've cited, or passages, were page 3 of the English translation: What have our first parliament experiences shown regarding national protection? We will have heavy fighting and so on. Then in the middle of the page: The present state of our unity is insufficient. And then going down to -- and then you also referred to the paragraph: Who says we can't create a Serbian state of sorts, which would be more appropriate and bring us closer to the achievement of our memorial ideals. So just to make clear my question, Mr. Treanor: It's really this, that you cited these passages at some length. I'm just asking what particular significance you -- if any, you attach to them which led you to draw specific attention to them.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in general terms, and without having read the -- and analysed the entire passage again, what I found interesting here is an indication at this early date that the -- at least one of the leaders of the SDS felt that they were running into problems already with this new coalition government they've established. They had a rather decisive victory over the previous ruling party, the League of Communists, whom the national parties feared might try to win the election by fraud, if by no other manner. They had -- the national parties had won the election and formed a coalition, and the outside observer might have thought they will live happily ever after. But this, as I say, is an early indication that the leaders of the SDS discovered quite quickly that this was not the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the concern about the outvoting, that had been there for some time, hadn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But they had come -- they had an agreement on forming a coalition, on distributing offices, and they may have felt, as indeed later on in the year Dr. Karadzic felt, and I think it came through in some of the documents we saw, that Mr. Izetbegovic, at least, had agreed that they would not do that. They would not force a decision on one of the other nationalities by outvoting. So there may have been at this date a perception that, as I put it earlier, that everything was going to be fine now and that the political agreement would prevent the outvoting, but Mr. Maksimovic seems to be forming the opinion that that particular danger is by no means over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the way he puts it is outvoting, treachery, rows, walkouts and protests, is that democracy? Mr. Treanor, you might say, well, yes, it is, mightn't you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You might.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Part and parcel, the normal feature of -- features of democracy?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: He seems to find that a bit disturbing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, he was actually right, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- well, without analysing the particular strategies and tactics he had in mind, in some substance that's exactly what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. The agreement never protected anybody, because eventually that is what Mr. Izetbegovic --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was certainly their perception, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you make another -- in your evidence -- this was at page 1307 of the transcript, just a very short reference, you say that -- well, you cite a passage in which Mr. Maksimovic is fearing treachery. And then you refer to -- he makes a reference to Herzegovina, which as you say is a reference to the fact that he perceives that the Croats in western Herzegovina would like to split off from BH and join Croatia perhaps. And he expresses his fear for what may happen in the Serbian part of Herzegovina. What you refer to as his perception that the Croats in western Herzegovina would like to split off from BH, that wasn't really just his perception that was at the time, wasn't it, that was clearly the position. Wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are a lot of Croats in western Herzegovina. Whether every single one of them wanted that, I don't know. That certainly was one of the main positions represented within the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You -- yes. Could we go to -- it will be the next volume, actually, number 2, at section 29. Just to remind ourselves what this is, this is the session, the second session of the SDS. Its second assembly is another way of referring to it in translation. On the 12th of July, 1991. I think it was exactly a year after the first one, wasn't it, Mr. Treanor?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, to the very day. And it's a fairly long record, because of course it was quite a large meeting. And then we go certainly not going to grind all through it, but if we go right on to page 55, and you dealt with this. It's at page 1337 of the transcript of your evidence. And then you say "he," which is Dr. Karadzic at this point: He gives some interesting remarks on the leadership of the party and its most prominent figures. And you say in this particular paragraph: We nevertheless have to name two of the delegates who have emerged as eminent political figures. And that's toward the bottom of page 55. It's about ten lines up. Do you see that: We nevertheless have to name two of the delegates? Do you see that passage?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, again, you -- interesting is a word that you perhaps not unnaturally use quite often throughout your evidence. What is the particular interest of his remarks?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's interesting that, within the context of a party meeting, he has singled out two leadership figures and identifies them by -- not by a role they play within the party but by roles they play within the official governing structure of BH.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krajisnik, because he identifies them as the speaker of the BH Assembly. That's what you have in mind first; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then Mr. Maksimovic as the president of the delegates club. And just remind us. The delegates club, what's the status of that, then?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we referred to it as the Deputies' Club.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Deputies' Club.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in the report. That is the organisation of the deputies from each particular political party represented within the Assembly. And they carry out certain business within the framework of the club. And the individual clubs are recognised within the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. I think I hadn't appreciated that's delegates club, that's not some new animal, then. That's simply a translation of --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the Deputies' Club.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Deputies' Club. So this is one of the three official or semi-official? What's the apt description of those really within --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Deputies' Clubs are mentioned within the Rules of Procedure of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. So official is fair?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: To that extent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Context.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're not constitutional or legislative -- legislatively created. Statutorily created bodies but within the --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just trying to get at what the particular point of interest is. Is it the fact that they're identified by reference to their positions, as you said a moment ago, in Bosnia-Herzegovina as opposed to their positions in the party, or some other point of interest?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he has identified to the party assembly two people who he -- whom he regards as being -- as having emerged as important leaders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, can we look at what -- this is quite a long -- other people get to speak as well, but Dr. Karadzic says a lot on this occasion, doesn't he?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at page 2, right at the very beginning, he greets all the delegates, that's all perfectly normal. They've sung the anthem, he greets all the delegates. He says at the foot of page 2: I would also like to greet the members of the SDS Political and Economic Council whose advice and suggestions have been crucial for the success of our policy. Do you see that? I'm sorry. Have I gone too fast? It's back --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Back at --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Back at page 2 of tab 29.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there's a plaudit for the -- was the Political and Economic Council a single organ then at that stage, so far as you're aware, or can you not say?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say definitely. As we've seen in the statutes, it refers to two different bodies, but later on, late in 1991, for instance, we just see references to the party council, as if there's only one now. So they may have been in fact melded into one at some point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Anyway, there's a plaudit for them, isn't there? Their advice and suggestions have been crucial for the success of our policy.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's well done Political and Economic Council. And then over the page, page 3, I would like -- top of the page: I would like to welcome the esteemed representatives of the press, and I want to thank them for the successful and fair coverage of our activities so far. So there's a plaudit for them as well, isn't there?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then if we go on to page 6, foot of page 6: From the date of its appointment until today, the Executive Committee has truly worked in adverse circumstances and in inadequate premises without a party of administrative apparatus and without the technical and other resources for its work. And then down towards to the middle of page 7: In the first phrase the Executive Committee tried to mobilise all the communities in BH as quickly as possible. And I'm going as slowly as possible. As quickly as possible in order to set up the municipal and local party branches. The efforts were made in highly adverse circumstances. The information and propaganda blockade had to be brought down and a number of other syndromes aimed against the Serbian people. That is why we can say that this part of the work was completed very successfully. So plaudits for the Executive Committee there?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then we go to page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, if you wouldn't mind if I interfere. I don't know whether your point would be, which I have in my mind already for quite some minutes, that everyone was applauded for doing a wonderful job and everyone was a rising star. Why don't ask the witness if that's your point. Of course if it's not your point, I'll listen to your next quotes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour. I did in the same way that we went through quite a lot of material here, I did want to make it and obtain Mr. Treanor's agreement. There's actually -- Your Honour, if I may, I'm practically there. If I may, one more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But then perhaps on your next subject, I don't know how many minutes it took to get us through this rather simple question. Just as the question or whether Mr. Treanor did not generalise too much where Mr. Karadzic said something about villages in Croatia and whether he generalised it for all villages. That very often takes us five to seven or eight minutes. The question is quite simple. After the first minute, it's entirely clear to everyone who listens carefully what the point is, and then I'm just wondering whether we could not hear the answer of the witness in a more speedy way. You just said I'm going as slowly as possible. I didn't took that as -- I took it as just referring to your speech at that moment. But I think a bit more tempo could --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course I was only referring to the way I was speaking. I'm certainly not going to enter into a squabble with the Tribunal about the speed. However, Your Honour, in the same way that considerable chunks of documents were placed on the record in the course of examination-in-chief, I am, with respect, Your Honour, while proceeding as quickly as I can, also going to do my job of placing certain items on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, as I told -- yes. Placing items on the record. But we could perhaps discuss that at a later stage. Could perhaps be done in a more speedy way. But it's just my feeling that we could proceed a little bit more quickly if the point is already clear, on from the, I would say, from the first 30 seconds. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, just for the record, then, at page 25, without dwelling on it, he complicated the Main Board for its work, and if one were to read through this document, which no doubt can be done but not right now, it's apparent. It's a political speech. It's a political leader's speech, isn't it, where he's -- prizes for everybody and encouragement and plaudits for everybody and every bit of the organisation. That's what it comes down to, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, two things. Yes, I think Dr. Karadzic is trying to give credit where credit is due.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or even sometimes, Mr. Treanor, I'm suggesting maybe even where it's not due, because that's what you do, encouragement. It's not -- he's actually telling everybody they've done a good job, which is what political leaders often do in public anyway, don't they?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me give the second part of my answer to the previous question. One portion that you read there I believe comes from the report by Velibor Ostojic, where he speaks about the boards doing a good job under difficult circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if that's right, then I stand corrected, Mr. Treanor, on that. That's particularly -- which page is that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: On page 7, pages 6 and 7.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 7.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're quite right. You're absolutely right, and I stand corrected on that.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I could just comment on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Velibor Ostojic, in his report, is I think trying to put a good face on things. He was the chairman, president of the Executive Board, elected the previous year. And I think it's apparent from this report and other things said at this meeting that there had been certain deficiencies in the work of the party organs and he in fact was not re-elected to that position. So his remarks are a little defensive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it's -- all it comes down to in the end is this, with that, that it's that the remarks that you particularly highlighted as interesting remarks and you picked out Mr. Krajisnik, and after all, we know why Mr. Krajisnik is here in court, it's actually of no interest, I suggest, beyond the fact that Mr. Krajisnik, as a whole list of other people and organs of the SDS, Mr. Krajisnik is included in the people who are given a pat on the back and told well done. There's no more to it than that, is there?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he's certainly included. I mean, I would -- if he had done a terrible job then maybe he might not have been included.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Treanor, you agree with what I said. There's no more to it than that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Than what?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Than that Mr. Krajisnik is included in the list of people who are given a pat on the back.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I say, I think that the indication that he and other people are given a pat on the back is an indication that Dr. Karadzic thinks that they've done a good job, as opposed to -- I mean, there are other people, as I indicated, that perhaps didn't do such a good job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the significance of the fact that he's referred to as the president of the Assembly of BH is just that when courtesies that are adopted in this particular society we're dealing with, as in many societies, you give somebody, if you're going to give them a title, you give them their official highest title, don't you, as the normal courtesy?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll illustrate what I mean. We refer to Her Majesty the Queen. We don't normally mention that she is the Duke of Normandy. That's all it is, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I take your point there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Or Queen of Australia, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Queens in different countries have different functions. Mr. Stewart, would this be a suitable moment to have our next break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll then have a break until five minutes to 1.00. And again, where you said that you would certainly not -- you expected not to go beyond the first eight binders, so therefore, we could feel confident with just the four with us at that very moment, was at that moment still very encouraging.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Certainly you're comfortably --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn until five minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, you took the Tribunal to the -- on occasions to the intercepts. There were various intercepts. And they are in a separate file, P66, I think is what it was numbered as. If we go to tab 2, please, Mr. Treanor. And this is apparently or purportedly a transcript of a conversation the 20th of June, between Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic. And -- or Dr. Karadzic. And you dealt with this in your evidence. The transcript reference is 1340 and 1341. And what I'm asking you, Mr. Treanor, is just this: That you drew the Tribunal's attention to this quite short transcript and you mentioned some of the people or you identified some of the people mentioned. But what is it that you extract of any interest or significance from this transcript?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, without reading the transcript over again --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why don't you do that, because actually it is very short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, in light of the passage of time since Mr. Treanor's examination-in-chief, I wonder if it might not also be of some assistance to the witness and might not facilitate this process if some reference is also made to the points he identified during the course of that examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, Mr. Tieger seems to ask you to point to what the witness already testified upon as far as the relevance or importance of this conversation is concerned, which might assist him in making up his mind on what might be missing or what needed further explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: By reference to the transcript?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I'm very happy to do that, Your Honour. It doesn't always work out that way, as we sometimes find. I was hoping to speed it by not doing that, but I can certainly do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you said in your evidence in chief was you observed that Mr. Krajisnik, Dr. Karadzic spoke to each other in the familiar form. You said the exact nature of what Mr. Krajisnik wanted to discuss with Dr. Karadzic wasn't clear but he wanted to meet him on what he regarded as an important matter. You identified Mr. Simovic as the highest-ranking SDS designated member of the government, deputy prime minister, Mr. Zepinic, who was the deputy minister of internal affairs, and Mr. Mandic, an SDS designated functionary in the BH Ministry of Internal Affairs. You said you believed he was an assistant minister. And then you said there was a series of conversations on that day which all revolve around setting up the same meeting among the various individuals involved. And that was it. So on that, I'm asking what -- how did I phrase my question originally? Just what of particular interest or significance you extract from that intercept or that transcript?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this intercept is an early example, I'm not sure if it's the earliest example, but an early example of consultations over the telephone between Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik. It illustrates, as I indicated, something about their relationship. They speak to each other in the familiar form, which Dr. Karadzic certainly doesn't do with everybody. There are -- there's at least one expletive in there, which indicates that they are indeed on very familiar terms and are quite comfortable speaking with each other. It mentions several other SDS officials, again if I can put it that way, within the government, indicating that consultations among the SDS officials in the government do take place, that they include Dr. Karadzic, who is not a government official, and include Mr. Krajisnik, who is not an official of the government per se, that is, in the former Yugoslav context, a member of the executive. It means an official, a deputy, and an official in the Assembly. So those are simply the points of interest there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And then can we go, then, to tab 6. I'm sorry. Tab 6 of that bundle, page 16. This is a conversation between Mr. Karadzic, or Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Miroslav, as he announces himself, from Banja Luka. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Just at page -- in fact, where we see -- we see an example of what I was referring to earlier just very briefly at page 11, don't we. About four lines down, we see a reference to "Krajisnik", which is not this Mr. Krajisnik. We won't go to it specially but it's in this document, page 11, fourth line. That's an example of what we're talking earlier?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just one point of clarification, if I may. Counsel is quite correct that the conversation begins with an exchange between Dr. Karadzic and Miroslav, but by the time it reaches page 16 of the translation, Dr. Karadzic is speaking with Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. The page 11 point, that's just an example of what we were talking about, isn't it, the fourth line?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see that in the English. I haven't found it in the B/C/S, but it undoubtedly is the point that you raised before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And then at -- so at page 16, whereas -- where Mr. Tieger helpfully observes, it's now a conversation between Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Brdjanin. It says therefore -- and Dr. Karadzic is saying in the middle: Therefore I said to the Main Board Slobo would get a gift of 20 billion dollars if only he gave up on us and then the answer is: I know that. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know anything about the 20 billion dollars. I can only infer that he's trying to get across the idea that a lot of people inside and perhaps outside of Yugoslavia would be happy if Mr. Milosevic did not support the SDS in its position in relation to remaining within Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is dollars just because it's a major currency or does it imply money coming from the United States? Can you say?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly wouldn't say the United States is being referred to in particular. I think -- yes, everyone knew what dollars were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And then -- the -- can we go back to the other bundles, please. This is file 2. I don't know whether that was the one you had in front of you. I think not yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we had already.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll go to 41, tab 41. And this is a decision of the 16th of December. It's a proclamation -- or it says it is, actually, a proclamation of the Autonomous Region of Krajina as an inseparable part of the federal state of federative Yugoslavia and an integral part of the federal unit of BH. And then you were asked -- this is at page 1399 of the transcript to explain the significance of various highlights, and in particular, you'd highlighted Articles 1, 2, and 3. And then -- I won't take time on Articles 1 and 2, but 3 states, and then -- well, we can see it. I don't have to read the whole thing, but it begins: Federal law regulations and other general legislation laws and regional legislation should be applied on the territory of the Autonomous Region of Krajina as well as legislation of BH not incompatible with this legislation. And then you say -- you drew attention to this at page 1401 of the transcript. The position is this, isn't it, that that is actually, when you cut through all the wording and what it's doing, it actually declares the existing legal position, doesn't it? I should say, Mr. Treanor, I'm not going into something highly technically here but it's quite clear it declares the existing legal position?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure what you mean by the existing legal position. What it does --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Should I clarify?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's all right. What it does, in my view, is it -- this autonomous region, which has -- the existence of which has no constitutional or statutory basis is giving -- appears to be giving itself in this Article the right to decide precisely that, what is the legal -- the existing legal position. That is, they seem to be giving themselves the right to decide when the laws of BH are in conflict with federal law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, as -- let's take it in stages. First of all, in terms, Article 3 says, doesn't it, that federal law shall be applied on the territory of the Autonomous Region of Krajina; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it does anyway at this time, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is September 1991. I'm not sure that in Slovenia and Croatia they were making such statements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, aren't we in BH here?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you said anywhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said anywhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm not following you, Mr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me -- Mr. Stewart, Mr. Treanor said: You referred to anywhere. He's referring to page 77, line 6, where you said: And it does anywhere at this time, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. My apologies, Mr. Treanor. I didn't mean anywhere in the world. I did mean -- I did mean, but I didn't make it sufficiently clear. I accept that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Actually, it applied anywhere within the Federation of Yugoslavia, didn't it, by definition?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, I'm not sure what the authorities in the republics of Slovenia and Croatia would have -- what position they would have taken on that issue at this particular point of time, in September of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think some of my confusion there, my co-counsel has just -- actually, what I said was it does anyway at this time, doesn't it. So that's why I was a bit puzzled. Because I didn't think I had said "anywhere". Perhaps that's a historical detail, but she thinks that I actually said "anyway", which is -- which would make sense of all the confusion in a sense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, Mr. Treanor, let's get back to where we are. This document relates to a territory, and I'm using that as an entirely neutral scriptive geographical word a territory part of Bosnia and Herzegovina at this time, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bosnia and Herzegovina at this time is part of the Federation of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So federal law applies.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it should.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the whole of -- I'm sorry. I'll make it clear to avoid the previous confusion. In the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina, including this particular territory where this document is concerned, federal law applies anyway, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should. It should.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you draw the distinction, Mr. Treanor, between --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I try to -- I feel that it's a legal issue, whether a law applies or is applied is not the same, and it seems that there's some confusion, and you, Mr. Stewart, as a lawyer, and Mr. Treanor as a non-lawyer, I'd like to make clearly the distinction that where the law applies it is on the theoretical level and whether it applies, which is on the practical level. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the light of His Honour's observation, Mr. Treanor, it technically applies -- it should, therefore, be applied as the law should. We're agreed so far?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The legislation of -- well, the laws, for that matter, of Bosnia-Herzegovina also apply or should apply --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- in that territory, but not, of course, when they're -- and I don't think this is a difficult legal point -- where they're inconsistent with the federal law, and I think you would know this, Mr. Treanor, that the federal law will override and that will apply, won't it? Or perhaps you don't know.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is precisely what is a contentious issue within Yugoslavia at this point in time. The republics, some of them, at least, were adopting various provisions, amendments to their constitution or statutes, saying things along this line, but in some cases the reverse. That is, federal law will not apply here if it's in conflict with our law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had any such statute at any such provision been passed or implemented in Bosnia-Herzegovina at this time?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in Bosnia. As I say, within the framework of larger Yugoslavia, this type of thing was happening. So that this is an issue, and they are taking here a particular position on that issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, again --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which, I admit, seems to be the obvious one, but there were other stances on that issue that were being taken by people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you -- what you said -- this is at page 1402 of the transcript, when you were following on from this point, by specific reference to this article in this document, you said: So here we see a very strong link between these -- this autonomous region, certainly, and the Federal State of Yugoslavia. That was your evidence?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was the way you described it. The link was very strong in this sense, wasn't it, that this autonomous region, as it had been declared, was in the Federal State of Yugoslavia, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About as clear a link as it's possible to get?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And it's clear from this that they wanted to remain within Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then at 43, same file, we've got a letter, and it's a letter of support to the federal secretary of National Defence, general of the army, that's Mr. Kadijevic. I'm not sure whether we met him before in the course of your evidence except in the reference to this document. And you said, again, to remind you, you drew the Tribunal's attention to this document and you said: This document is reflective of two things in particular that I'd like to point out. One is the continued support for the Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA. As the Court will remember, that figured very early on in the programme of the SDS and continues during this period of hostilities in Croatia. And just without going at all into the details of it, Mr. Treanor, hostilities in connection with Croatia at that time were severe, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In September? Yes, I think they can be safely characterised that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say: I think we've alluded earlier to assistance in mobilisation and that sort of thing and by the SDS and, on the other hand, the opposition or reluctance of the other two parties in the governing coalition, the SDA and the HDZ, to support those military operations. Well, again, the underlying politics is perhaps very clear, but absolutely at its simplest, those military operations involved the JNA, the army of Yugoslavia, federal Yugoslavia, in military operations, and support coming from the SDS as a major party in the constituent part of the federal Yugoslavia, or the army of the country that it was in. That's it in a nutshell, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: They support the JNA, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In a nutshell, they're supporting the army of the state to which they belong and which they're in?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whereas the SDA and the HDZ are in fact not supporting the military operations of the army of the state that they are in?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we then turn to tab 44. No, I'm sorry. We have to go back to the intercepts bundle again at 14. And you drew attention -- this is a transcript of a conversation between Dr. Karadzic and -- I think it's doctor, actually Dr. Plavsic, and you drew attention particularly to the passage in the middle of the second page, where Dr. Karadzic is -- refers to right in the middle of the page, until in the SUP it appoints -- I mean, until they stop deciding where shall each individual Serb work. And Mrs. Plavsic -- Dr. Plavsic says: Yes, exactly as long as they don't stop determining. And you said -- in your evidence you said: So he's not happy with the way even Serbs are being appointed. And you say: And we do have a lot of information on this subject but here is reflected the concern that I mentioned. And the concern -- you said that the SDS was not getting to determine which Serbs would work where. And then Judge Orie said: Yes. And you read that in until in the SUP it appoints that passage I just mentioned. I mean, until they stop deciding where shall each individual Serb work. And you said: Yes, I would render that as where which Serb will work. So it's a selection of or a question of selecting people and the place that they will work. I'm actually just really asking where you get that from, Mr. Treanor. On the face of this document, it doesn't support what you're saying there. Perhaps you can explain where you get that from.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. Where do I get what from?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your conclusion there. You would render that as them deciding where -- the way you put it is where which Serb will work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which page of the transcript we are exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. It's 1407.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you had also expressed it as them being concerned about not being able to determine which Serbs would work where. Now --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the one issue is strictly a translation issue, how to translate that particular phrase.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you would need to go back to the B/C/S for that, would you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you then please read it in B/C/S, Mr. Treanor, so that we receive translation in English and can compare it with what's on paper.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until an appointment is made to the SUP, until they stop appointing, or rather, determining where which Serb will work.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I don't think I'm going to get any further with this, Mr. Treanor. I think I know when I'm beaten by the general fog surrounding a particular point. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In file 2, at tab 44, which was the last one - we were just coming to that - this is instruction to municipal communities of the SDS, and it comes from Dr. Karadzic. The wartime forces of the police are currently being mobilised. There are rumours that up to a hundred per cent of the force are being mobilised, although the bodies at the republic level can mobilise only 50 per cent. There are also rumours that only Muslims are being called up or that Serbs do not heed the call-up, which would result in a Muslim police force. Are you able to say - if you're not, Mr. Treanor, you're not - are you able to say whether at that time those rumours were in fact well-founded?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. Well, I'm not sure what the rumours are. No. I've seen other -- there are other documents about this. Maybe we had another one. There was a document that I -- we may have used, indicating that perhaps a slightly later date, that it was -- Dr. Karadzic might have thought it was a good idea that Serbs do heed the call-up. The nature of the rumours being referred to here are rather imprecise and slightly contradictory, that only Muslims are being called up or that Serbs did not heed the call. I think all I can say is that I do believe there was a call-up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Treanor. If we turn now -- we can put -- well, we've finished 2. We can put that bundle 2 aside and go to 3. And this -- well, this is I think something you described -- you dealt with this at page 1421. It is in the transcript, it's something you described as the October 16th memorandum. Actually, it seems to be dated the 14th, but we occasionally get these discrepancies in date. But you drew attention to item 2, that BH will continue -- well, I should say at the top of the first page pursuant to Article 3, paragraph 2 of the Rules of Procedure of the Assembly of the Republika Srpska, the Assembly of SRBH, at a joint session of the Chambers of the Assembly of SRBH on 14th October 1991 adopted the following and so on. And then 2, BH --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, if you put your microphone off. Then you can't blame us for overhearing. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You drew attention to item 2 on the second page: "BH will continue to advocate the survival of the Yugoslav community on new foundations acceptable to all. In the meantime, she will also advocate the proper functioning of existing joint institutions. Our representatives will not attend sessions of the Assembly and Presidency of the Federation of Yugoslavia if they aren't attended by representatives of all republics." And the position at that time was this, wasn't it, that it was in fact quite clear that Croatia were not attending, so that, in effect, given that context, that Croatia were not attending, it was absolutely clear that the -- that Bosnia-Herzegovina would also not be represented?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would say that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said in your evidence - this is at page 1422 - you said: "Now, as I've indicated, Croatia was in fact, and I think in law, independent at this time, so whatever relationship BH was going to have with Serbia under that provision, it would certainly not include being part of ..." And then your evidence said: "... not include being part of a federal state with Serbia." Now, I apologise. You haven't actually got this piece of paper in front of you. But that doesn't make sense, does it, Mr. Treanor? I suggest you must have intended to say: Would certainly not include being part of a federal state with Croatia. Do you follow me?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's a little bit hard, because you've --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The meaning, if I'm recollecting correctly, is the following: As you indicated -- as you indicated that I indicated, Croatia was independent by this time. And I think that -- and this is just something I, you know, I've understood, that the -- October the 9th is the date that -- from which Croatia is considered, perhaps in retrospect, to have gained its independence. There was a three-month moratorium on independence imposed, or agreed to, in early July, so that had run out. So Croatia is out of Yugoslavia now. And so the implication of this is that since we're going to maintain the same relationship with Croatia -- with Serbia as we do with Croatia, and Croatia is out of Yugoslavia, then, therefore, we will not be in Yugoslavia either, because Serbia is in that state. So we will not be in the same state with Serbia, because we're obviously not going to be in the same state with Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I think I should correct myself on the transcript, actually, because I -- I think I -- I think I referred to Republika Srpska. What I meant to say Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's a few lines back. Then paragraph 4. BH was going to do everything -- this is the fifth line: "BH will do everything in its power to remain neutral in the conflict, which means that her citizens would not be engaged on either side and her territory would not be used for war." Of course, that conflict was the conflict between Croatia and Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you said that that was -- you thought it fair to say the SDS leadership took violent exception to that, and that, in effect, the memorandum -- and then you said you didn't - still 1422 of the transcript - you didn't want to overstate this, but in effect, it announced the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. My question is this: that that -- in your view, that would have been clearly understood, would it, by the Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and particularly the SDS at the time?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was an absolute crystal-clear message?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.
