utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you pointed out in your evidence earlier on this same page, you said that this -- well, Mr. Treanor, to say that this is not at all to the liking of the SDS leadership, that would be an admirable understatement, wouldn't it, to say --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether it's admirable or not, I'm not sure. But yes, I could call that an understatement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they -- in fact, you said they were, of course, extremely angry, and they were angry at the manner, wasn't it, weren't they, because they thought they had the agreement of Mr. Izetbegovic, as you said, but this was a complete U-turn by Mr. Izetbegovic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, It certainly seemed so to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, It was, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if Mr. Izetbegovic was telling his people what he had or had not agreed with Dr. Karadzic. I know, and presented here, what Dr. Karadzic thought their understanding was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me clarify, then, Mr. Treanor. You're quite right. It may be that as far as his private communications with his own party were concerned, it was a naught-degree turn by Mr. Izetbegovic. But as far as what he had said to the SDS was concerned and what he had agreed with the SDS, this was 180-degree turn, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It certainly seems, from what we've seen in these documents on the Serbian attitude, that they definitely regarded it in that light.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, the agreement that they had had with Mr. Izetbegovic had -- it had been broken by Mr. Izetbegovic, hadn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if that was the agreement, I would say, without having seen any other possibly relevant documentation, that's the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then if we go to 47 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just a minor point of clarification. I don't think the record today indicates that the memorandum to which counsel was referring was located at tab 46, and I just wanted to make that explicit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now it is on record.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I do not know how much time you would need for 47. If it would be more than two or three minutes, then I'd rather adjourn until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, with respect, I would -- I'd rather the Tribunal adjourn until tomorrow on that point, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Usually I try to get organised after we adjourn, but this time I changed the order. Madam Registrar, tomorrow we'll sit where and at what time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm asking it because we were scheduled for tomorrow to sit in this same courtroom at 9.00 in the morning. On Thursday, however, we were scheduled to sit in the afternoon, but there is a possibility to sit in the morning, if everyone can adapt his agenda to that. I can imagine that, for example, visits to Mr. Krajisnik could oppose to a change of schedule at such short notice. So, therefore, I'd like to know as soon as possible from the parties whether they'd prefer and whether they are able to sit in the morning next Thursday. If you can give me the answer right away, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I hope -- I can give you this answer right away, Your Honour. We have no objection to sitting on Thursday morning. However, Your Honour, please, on my side, may I know as soon as possible, because I have to rearrange various things as a result of that change.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I see there's, as such, no opposition, but you'd like to know as soon as possible. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, because then I simply -- I have to rearrange something that I will rearrange, but I do need to know, please, soon, in order to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, is the position of the Defence already known?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, it's no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Prosecution, I'm sorry. No problem for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are good chances. The only one that has to check his agenda is myself. So I'll let you know immediately after the adjournment. You can ask Mr. Acquaviva or Ms. Philpott whether we'll sit in the morning or in the afternoon. . But I first have to check it. We'll then adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
